about: Paper 13, Law of Tort, is one of the first-year papers of the Cambridge Law Tripos. According to the Faculty, it deals with civil wrongs for which one person can sue another, usually for compensation, with negligence as its main focus, alongside occupiers' liability, private nuisance, manufacturers' liability for defective products, trespass to the person, the allocation of liability between two or more wrongdoers, and an employer's liability for its staff. The Faculty stresses the debate over when the law should intervene and how it balances competing rights. This pack follows the Faculty's topic list, with negligence split into duty, special duty problems, breach, and causation, remoteness and defences.

notes.body:
A tort is a civil wrong for which the person wronged can sue, usually for compensation. Negligence is the centre of the Cambridge course. To succeed the claimant must show: (1) a duty of care, (2) breach, (3) damage caused by the breach, and (4) that the damage is not too remote, subject to defences. All references are to the law of England and Wales.

The starting point
- Donoghue v Stevenson [1932] AC 562 (HL): a manufacturer owed a duty to the ultimate consumer of a bottle of ginger beer allegedly containing a decomposed snail. Lord Atkin's 'neighbour principle': take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure persons so closely and directly affected that you ought to have them in contemplation.
- Anns v Merton LBC [1978] AC 728 proposed a broad two-stage test (proximity, then policy reasons to negate). It was overruled in Murphy v Brentwood DC [1991] 1 AC 398.
- Caparo Industries plc v Dickman [1990] 2 AC 605: auditors owed no duty to investors buying shares in reliance on the accounts. The House stressed foreseeability, proximity and whether it is fair, just and reasonable to impose a duty, together with incremental development by analogy.

The modern approach
Robinson v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire Police [2018] UKSC 4 held that Caparo does not lay down a three-stage test to be applied in every case.
- Where a case falls within an established category (e.g. driver to other road users, doctor to patient, employer to employee), the existing law applies.
- In a novel case the court develops the law incrementally by analogy with established categories, asking whether a duty would be fair, just and reasonable.
- Police officers arresting a suspect in a busy street owed a duty to a pedestrian injured in the struggle, because they created the danger by a positive act.

Acts and omissions
The law distinguishes making things worse (a positive act causing harm) from failing to confer a benefit (an omission). There is generally no duty to prevent harm or to protect others from third parties: Smith v Littlewoods Organisation Ltd [1987] AC 241. Recognised exceptions include:
- an assumption of responsibility by the defendant;
- control over the third party: Home Office v Dorset Yacht Co Ltd [1970] AC 1004 (borstal officers and escaping trainees);
- the defendant creating the danger;
- control of land or a dangerous thing from which the danger arises.

Public authorities and the police
Public bodies are generally subject to the same principles as private persons, so they are not liable merely for failing to use statutory powers to confer a benefit.
- Stovin v Wise [1996] AC 923 and Gorringe v Calderdale MBC [2004] UKHL 15: no duty arising merely from statutory powers to improve road safety.
- Michael v Chief Constable of South Wales Police [2015] UKSC 2: no duty to a woman killed after a 999 call was mishandled; the police had not assumed responsibility to her.
- Poole BC v GN [2019] UKSC 25: a council that had housed a family next to abusive neighbours, and investigated the children's welfare, owed the children no duty to protect them from the neighbours (for example by taking them into care), since it had not assumed responsibility for them.
- Tindall v Chief Constable of Thames Valley Police [2024] UKSC 33: police who attended an icy road and left without making it safe owed no duty to a later motorist, because they had not made matters worse.

How to answer a duty question
1. Is there an established category? If so, say so briefly and move on.
2. Is the harm caused by an act or an omission (or by a third party)? If omission, look for an exception.
3. Is the loss of a special type (psychiatric harm, pure economic loss)? Apply the special rules.
4. Only for a genuinely novel situation, reason by analogy and consider policy.

Exam tips: do not recite 'the Caparo three-stage test' as the universal test; the examiners expect Robinson. Spend your time on the contested element in the facts.

notes.h: Duty of care: psychiatric harm and pure economic loss
notes.body:
Where the claimant suffers psychiatric injury or purely financial loss, the courts impose extra control mechanisms on the duty of care, mainly to limit the number and range of potential claimants.

Psychiatric harm
The claimant must have a recognised psychiatric illness; ordinary grief, fear or distress is not enough.

Primary victims
A primary victim is someone within the range of foreseeable physical injury. Page v Smith [1996] AC 155: a claimant in a minor car crash who suffered a recurrence of chronic fatigue syndrome could recover, because physical injury to him was foreseeable, even though psychiatric injury was not.

Secondary victims
A secondary victim suffers psychiatric injury from witnessing injury or danger to another. Alcock v Chief Constable of South Yorkshire Police [1992] 1 AC 310 (Hillsborough) set the controls:
- a close tie of love and affection with the person endangered (presumed for parents, children and spouses; must otherwise be proved);
- proximity in time and space to the accident or its immediate aftermath;
- perception of it with the claimant's own unaided senses (watching television was not enough);
- psychiatric injury must be foreseeable in a person of reasonable fortitude.
McLoughlin v O'Brian [1983] 1 AC 410: a mother who saw her family at hospital about two hours after a crash, before they were cleaned up, was within the 'immediate aftermath'.
White v Chief Constable of South Yorkshire Police [1999] 2 AC 455: police officers who tended Hillsborough victims were not primary victims merely as employees or rescuers; a rescuer must be exposed to physical danger, or reasonably believe they are.
Paul v Royal Wolverhampton NHS Trust [2024] UKSC 1: the Supreme Court held that relatives who witnessed a family member's death or medical crisis caused by an earlier negligent failure to diagnose could not recover as secondary victims. Recovery requires witnessing an accident, in the ordinary sense of an unexpected and unintended event causing injury (or a risk of injury) by violent external means, or its immediate aftermath. The Court also rejected any requirement of a 'sudden shock' or a 'horrifying event'.

Pure economic loss
Pure economic loss is financial loss not consequential on physical damage to the claimant's person or property. The general rule is that it is not recoverable when caused by a negligent act.
- Spartan Steel & Alloys Ltd v Martin & Co [1973] QB 27 (CA): contractors cut a power cable. The claimant recovered for the damaged melt and the profit on it (consequential loss), but not for profits on melts it could not process during the power cut (pure economic loss).
- Murphy v Brentwood DC [1991] 1 AC 398: the cost of repairing a defective house, or its loss of value, is pure economic loss, not damage to property.

The Hedley Byrne exception
Hedley Byrne & Co Ltd v Heller & Partners Ltd [1964] AC 465: a duty can arise for negligent statements where there is a special relationship involving reliance and an assumption of responsibility. On the facts the bank's disclaimer prevented liability; today such disclaimers are tested under the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 or the Consumer Rights Act 2015.
- Caparo [1990]: a statement made to the general public, or for a different purpose, does not ground a duty.
- Smith v Eric S Bush [1990] 1 AC 831: a mortgage valuer owed a duty to the house buyer who would foreseeably rely on the valuation; the disclaimer failed the UCTA reasonableness test.
- Henderson v Merrett Syndicates Ltd [1995] 2 AC 145: the principle extends to services, and liability in tort can run concurrently with contract.
- White v Jones [1995] 2 AC 207: a solicitor who negligently failed to draw up a will in time was liable to the intended beneficiaries.
- Spring v Guardian Assurance plc [1995] 2 AC 296: an employer giving a reference owed a duty to the employee who was its subject.
- Customs and Excise Commissioners v Barclays Bank plc [2006] UKHL 28: a bank notified of a freezing injunction owed no duty to the party who obtained it; it had not assumed responsibility.

Exam tips: classify the claimant first (primary or secondary victim; consequential or pure economic loss). For secondary victims, go through each Alcock control in turn and now consider whether there was an 'accident' in the Paul sense.

Once a duty is established, the question is whether the defendant fell below the standard of care. This is a question of fact judged objectively.

The reasonable person
Negligence is the failure to do what a reasonable person would do, or doing what a prudent and reasonable person would not do: Blyth v Birmingham Waterworks Co (1856) 11 Ex 781. The standard is objective and does not bend to the defendant's own inexperience.
- Nettleship v Weston [1971] 2 QB 691 (CA): a learner driver is judged by the standard of a reasonably competent driver.
- Wells v Cooper [1958] 2 QB 265 (CA): a householder doing his own carpentry was judged as a reasonably competent amateur, not a professional joiner.
- Mullin v Richards [1998] 1 WLR 1304 (CA): a 15-year-old was judged against a reasonable 15-year-old; the injury from a play fight with plastic rulers was not foreseeable to such a child.

Factors in setting the standard
Courts weigh several factors in deciding what reasonable care required.
- Likelihood of harm: Bolton v Stone [1951] AC 850 (HL). A cricket ball struck a passer-by; balls had left the ground only about six times in some thirty years, so the risk was so small that a reasonable person could disregard it.
- Seriousness of harm: Paris v Stepney BC [1951] AC 367 (HL). An employer should have provided goggles to a worker with one eye because the consequences of injury to his good eye were especially grave.
- Cost and practicability of precautions: Latimer v AEC Ltd [1953] AC 643 (HL). After a flood made a factory floor slippery, the employer spread sawdust; closing the factory was not required.
- Social value of the activity: Watt v Hertfordshire CC [1954] 1 WLR 835 (CA). Fire services taking a risk to save life were not negligent in transporting a heavy jack in an unsuitable lorry.
- Statute reinforces this: the Compensation Act 2006 s 1 allows the court to consider whether requiring steps would prevent a desirable activity. The Social Action, Responsibility and Heroism Act 2015 requires the court to consider whether the defendant acted for the benefit of society, took a generally responsible approach, or acted heroically in an emergency.

Knowledge at the time
The defendant is judged by the state of knowledge when they acted, not with hindsight: Roe v Minister of Health [1954] 2 QB 66 (CA), where anaesthetic was contaminated through invisible cracks in ampoules, a risk not then known.

Professionals
- Bolam v Friern Hospital Management Committee [1957] 1 WLR 582: a doctor is not negligent if acting in accordance with a practice accepted as proper by a responsible body of medical opinion, even if others would differ.
- Bolitho v City and Hackney HA [1998] AC 232 (HL): the court must be satisfied that the professional opinion has a logical basis and withstands analysis.
- Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015] UKSC 11: Bolam does not govern advice on risks. A doctor must take reasonable care to ensure the patient knows of any material risks and of reasonable alternative treatments. A risk is material if a reasonable person in the patient's position would be likely to attach significance to it, or the doctor knows or should know that this patient would.
- McCulloch v Forth Valley Health Board [2023] UKSC 26: whether an alternative treatment is 'reasonable' (and so must be mentioned) is judged by the professional standard in Bolam.

Proving breach
The claimant bears the burden on the balance of probabilities. Where an accident would not ordinarily happen without negligence and the thing was under the defendant's control, the court may infer negligence (res ipsa loquitur): Scott v London and St Katharine Docks Co (1865) 3 H & C 596, where bags of sugar fell from a warehouse.

Exam tips: identify the precaution the defendant should have taken and weigh the factors explicitly. For medical facts, separate treatment (Bolam/Bolitho) from disclosure of risks (Montgomery).

Even a careless defendant is liable only for damage that the breach caused and that is not too remote, and damages may be reduced or barred by defences.

Factual causation: the 'but for' test
Would the damage have occurred but for the breach? Barnett v Chelsea and Kensington HMC [1969] 1 QB 428: a doctor negligently failed to examine a man who had drunk arsenic, but he would have died anyway, so the breach did not cause the death.

Departures from 'but for'
- Material contribution to injury: Bonnington Castings Ltd v Wardlaw [1956] AC 613. Negligent dust that made a more than minimal contribution to lung disease sufficed.
- Material increase in risk: McGhee v National Coal Board [1973] 1 WLR 1, where the lack of washing facilities increased the risk of dermatitis.
- Wilsher v Essex AHA [1988] AC 1074 confined McGhee: with five possible causes of a baby's blindness, the claimant had to prove causation on the balance of probabilities.
- Fairchild v Glenhaven Funeral Services Ltd [2002] UKHL 22: for mesothelioma caused by asbestos exposure with several negligent employers, each employer that materially increased the risk was liable.
- Barker v Corus UK Ltd [2006] UKHL 20 made Fairchild liability proportionate to the risk created. Parliament reversed this for mesothelioma by the Compensation Act 2006 s 3, which makes such defendants jointly and severally liable.
- Loss of a chance: Hotson v East Berkshire AHA [1987] AC 750 and Gregg v Scott [2005] UKHL 2 deny recovery for a lost chance of a better medical outcome in personal injury cases where the claimant cannot prove causation on the balance of probabilities.
- Chester v Afshar [2004] UKHL 41: a patient not warned of a small risk recovered on policy grounds (autonomy), though she would probably have had the operation later anyway.

Intervening acts (novus actus interveniens)
- Third party: a truly independent act may break the chain, e.g. a police inspector's negligent order in Knightley v Johns [1982] 1 WLR 349.
- Claimant's own conduct: McKew v Holland & Hannen & Cubitts (Scotland) Ltd [1969] 3 All ER 1621 (unreasonably descending steep stairs with a weakened leg). Contrast Corr v IBC Vehicles Ltd [2008] UKHL 13: suicide caused by accident-induced depression did not break the chain.

Remoteness
The Wagon Mound (No 1) [1961] AC 388 (PC) rejected the 'direct consequences' test of Re Polemis [1921] 3 KB 560: the defendant is liable only for damage of a kind or type that was reasonably foreseeable.
- Hughes v Lord Advocate [1963] AC 837: the precise manner of harm need not be foreseen (burns from an unforeseeable lamp explosion were still burns).
- Jolley v Sutton LBC [2000] 1 WLR 1082: it was foreseeable that children would meddle with an abandoned boat, so injury when it fell on a boy jacking it up was within the risk.
- The eggshell skull rule: once some harm of the foreseeable type occurs, the defendant takes the claimant as found. Smith v Leech Brain & Co Ltd [1962] 2 QB 405: a burn to the lip triggered cancer in a pre-disposed worker.

Defences
- Contributory negligence: the Law Reform (Contributory Negligence) Act 1945 s 1(1) reduces damages to the extent the court thinks just and equitable having regard to the claimant's share in responsibility. Froom v Butcher [1976] QB 286 suggested 25% for failing to wear a seat belt if it would have prevented the injury entirely, 15% if it would have reduced it. A 100% reduction is not possible (Pitts v Hunt [1991] 1 QB 24).
- Voluntary assumption of risk (volenti): requires full knowledge and free agreement to the risk, e.g. Morris v Murray [1991] 2 QB 6 (flight with an obviously drunk pilot). The Road Traffic Act 1988 s 149 prevents a driver relying on a passenger's consent in cases requiring compulsory insurance.
- Illegality: Henderson v Dorset Healthcare University NHS Foundation Trust [2020] UKSC 43, applying Gray v Thames Trains Ltd [2009] UKHL 33, barred a claim for losses flowing from the claimant's own manslaughter conviction.

Exam tips: treat each head separately, and use Fairchild-type reasoning only where the facts truly fit (single agent, scientific uncertainty).

Occupiers' liability concerns injury caused by the state of premises. It is governed by two statutes in England and Wales: the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957 for visitors and the Occupiers' Liability Act 1984 for others, chiefly trespassers.

Who is an occupier?
The Acts adopt the common law. An occupier is anyone with a sufficient degree of control over the premises: Wheat v E Lacon & Co Ltd [1966] AC 552 (HL). There can be more than one occupier.

The 1957 Act: visitors
- Visitors are those who would at common law be invitees or licensees, i.e. those with express or implied permission (s 1(2)). Exceeding the limits of permission makes the entrant a trespasser.
- s 2(1): the occupier owes all visitors the 'common duty of care', except so far as he can and does extend, restrict, modify or exclude it by agreement or otherwise.
- s 2(2): the duty is to take such care as in all the circumstances is reasonable to see that the visitor will be reasonably safe in using the premises for the purposes for which he is invited or permitted to be there.
- s 2(3)(a): an occupier must be prepared for children to be less careful than adults. Glasgow Corporation v Taylor [1922] 1 AC 44 (poisonous berries as an allurement); Phipps v Rochester Corporation [1955] 1 QB 450 (an occupier may expect very young children to be accompanied by their parents).
- s 2(3)(b): an occupier may expect a person exercising a calling to guard against risks ordinarily incident to it. Roles v Nathan [1963] 1 WLR 1117: chimney sweeps killed by fumes they had been warned about.
- s 2(4)(a): a warning discharges the duty only if, in all the circumstances, it was enough to enable the visitor to be reasonably safe.
- s 2(4)(b): an occupier is not liable for faulty work by an independent contractor if he acted reasonably in entrusting the work and took reasonable steps to check the contractor's competence and, where appropriate, that the work was properly done. Compare Haseldine v CA Daw & Son Ltd [1941] 2 KB 343 (technical lift repairs) with Woodward v Mayor of Hastings [1945] KB 174 (an icy step, easily checked).
- s 2(5): no duty for risks willingly accepted by the visitor.
- Liability for death or personal injury from negligence cannot be excluded by business occupiers (Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 s 2) or against consumers (Consumer Rights Act 2015 s 65).

The 1984 Act: non-visitors
- s 1(3): a duty is owed only if the occupier (a) is aware of the danger or has reasonable grounds to believe it exists; (b) knows or has reasonable grounds to believe that the other is in, or may come into, the vicinity of the danger; and (c) the risk is one against which, in all the circumstances, he may reasonably be expected to offer some protection.
- s 1(4): the duty is to take such care as is reasonable in all the circumstances to see that the person does not suffer injury on the premises by reason of the danger.
- s 1(5): the duty may be discharged by reasonable steps to give warning or to discourage people from incurring the risk.
- s 1(6): no duty for risks willingly accepted.
- s 1(8): no liability for loss of or damage to property.

Obvious risks and free choices
Tomlinson v Congleton BC [2003] UKHL 47: a young man broke his neck diving into a shallow lake in a park. There was no liability: the danger came from his own choice of an obviously risky activity, not the state of the premises, and prevention would have meant destroying a valued amenity. Similar reasoning appears in Ratcliff v McConnell [1999] 1 WLR 670 (diving into a closed pool at night) and Keown v Coventry Healthcare NHS Trust [2006] EWCA Civ 39 (a child climbing a fire escape: the danger came from his activity, not the premises).

Exam tips: first classify the entrant (visitor or trespasser), then identify the occupier, then apply the right Act section by section. Remember that the 1984 Act does not cover property damage.

Private nuisance protects a person's use and enjoyment of land from unreasonable interference by a neighbour. The Faculty's own illustration, the right to play cricket against the right not to be hit by a cricket ball, captures the balancing involved.

Kinds of nuisance
- Encroachment on the claimant's land (e.g. roots or Japanese knotweed).
- Physical damage to the land or buildings.
- Interference with the quiet enjoyment of land (noise, smells, smoke, vibration).
Network Rail Infrastructure Ltd v Williams [2018] EWCA Civ 1514: knotweed roots impairing the use and enjoyment of land were actionable before physical damage.

Who can sue?
Hunter v Canary Wharf Ltd [1997] AC 655 (HL): nuisance is a tort against land, so the claimant needs a proprietary interest or exclusive possession (e.g. owner or tenant). Family members and lodgers without such an interest cannot sue. The same case held that interference with television reception by a tall building was not actionable, as a landowner is generally free to build on his own land.

Who can be sued?
- The creator of the nuisance.
- The occupier who adopts or continues a nuisance created by a trespasser or by nature: Sedleigh-Denfield v O'Callaghan [1940] AC 880 (a blocked drainage pipe installed by a trespasser); Leakey v National Trust [1980] QB 485 (natural landslips; a 'measured duty' depending on the occupier's resources).
- A landlord only if he authorised the nuisance (for example by letting for a purpose almost certain to cause it) or participated directly in it: Coventry v Lawrence (No 2) [2014] UKSC 46.

Unreasonableness
The question is whether the interference is unreasonable, judged by what ordinary people would tolerate, not whether the defendant took care. Relevant factors:
- Character of the neighbourhood: Sturges v Bridgman (1879) 11 Ch D 852, 'what would be a nuisance in Belgrave Square would not necessarily be so in Bermondsey'. Locality is irrelevant where there is material physical damage: St Helen's Smelting Co v Tipping (1865) 11 HL Cas 642.
- Duration, frequency and time of day.
- Abnormal sensitivity: Robinson v Kilvert (1889) 41 Ch D 88; now framed as foreseeability (Network Rail v Morris [2004] EWCA Civ 172).
- Malice: Christie v Davey [1893] 1 Ch 316 (deliberately banging on the party wall); Hollywood Silver Fox Farm Ltd v Emmett [1936] 2 KB 468 (firing guns to disrupt breeding foxes).
- Fearn v Board of Trustees of the Tate Gallery [2023] UKSC 4: the Supreme Court held that constant viewing into neighbouring flats from a public viewing platform was a nuisance. The key question is whether the defendant's use is a common and ordinary use of land; if not, and it substantially interferes with the ordinary use of neighbouring land, it is actionable.

Foreseeability and damages
Cambridge Water Co Ltd v Eastern Counties Leather plc [1994] 2 AC 264: damages are recoverable only for harm of a reasonably foreseeable type. Davies v Bridgend CBC [2024] UKSC 15: a claimant could not recover for diminution in value from knotweed where that loss had already been suffered before the defendant's breach began, so it was not caused by the breach.

Defences and non-defences
- Prescription: a nuisance actionable continuously for 20 years may be legitimised (Sturges v Bridgman).
- Statutory authority: Allen v Gulf Oil Refining Ltd [1981] AC 1001.
- Coming to the nuisance is not a defence: Sturges v Bridgman; Miller v Jackson [1977] QB 966; Coventry v Lawrence [2014] UKSC 13.
- Planning permission is not a defence in itself, though it may be relevant to the character of the locality: Coventry v Lawrence.
- Public benefit is not a defence to liability but may affect the remedy. In Miller v Jackson a majority of the Court of Appeal (Geoffrey Lane and Cumming-Bruce LJJ) found the cricket club liable, but a differently composed majority (Lord Denning MR and Cumming-Bruce LJ) refused an injunction and awarded damages.

Remedies
Injunction is the usual remedy. Shelfer v City of London Electric Lighting Co [1895] 1 Ch 287 limited damages in lieu of an injunction to exceptional cases; Coventry v Lawrence held that the court's discretion is wider and should not be fettered mechanically by Shelfer. Abatement (self-help) is available in limited cases.

Exam tips: work through standing, defendant, unreasonableness factors, then defences and remedies. Always ask whether the damage is physical (locality irrelevant) or amenity-based.

A person injured by a defective product in England and Wales may sue in negligence or, more often, under the strict liability regime in Part I of the Consumer Protection Act 1987 (CPA), which implemented Directive 85/374/EEC.

Common law negligence
- Donoghue v Stevenson [1932] AC 562: a manufacturer owes a duty to the ultimate consumer where the product reaches them in the form in which it left the manufacturer, with no reasonable possibility of intermediate examination.
- Grant v Australian Knitting Mills Ltd [1936] AC 85 (PC): negligence was inferred where underwear containing excess sulphites caused dermatitis.
- Proving fault is hard for complex products, which is the main reason for the CPA.

Who is liable under the CPA (s 2)
Where damage is caused wholly or partly by a defect in a product, liability falls on:
- the producer: the manufacturer, or whoever won or abstracted a substance or carried out a process giving the product its essential characteristics (s 1(2));
- an 'own-brander', who holds himself out as the producer by putting his name or trade mark on the product (s 2(2)(b));
- the person who imported the product into the United Kingdom in the course of business to supply it to another (s 2(2)(c), as amended after Brexit);
- a supplier, if the claimant asks within a reasonable time for the producer, own-brander or importer to be identified and the supplier fails within a reasonable time to identify them or its own supplier (s 2(3)).
Liability is joint and several where more than one person is liable.

Defect (s 3)
A product is defective if its safety is not such as persons generally are entitled to expect. All the circumstances are considered, including:
- how and for what purposes it was marketed, its get-up, and any instructions or warnings;
- what might reasonably be expected to be done with it;
- the time when the producer supplied it.

Interpreting 'defect'
- A v National Blood Authority [2001] 3 All ER 289 (Burton J): blood infected with hepatitis C was defective. The public was entitled to expect blood to be free from infection; the fact that the risk was unavoidable was irrelevant to whether there was a defect.
- Wilkes v DePuy International Ltd [2016] EWHC 3096 (QB) (Hickinbottom J) preferred a flexible, holistic assessment in which a product's risks and benefits, including avoidability, may be relevant.

Defences (s 4)
- (a) the defect is attributable to compliance with a legal requirement;
- (b) the defendant did not supply the product to another;
- (c) the supply was not in the course of business (and not with a view to profit);
- (d) the defect did not exist at the relevant time;
- (e) the 'development risks' defence: the state of scientific and technical knowledge at the relevant time was not such that a producer of similar products might be expected to have discovered the defect. In A v National Blood Authority it failed because the risk was known, even if undetectable in particular units. In Abouzaid v Mothercare (UK) Ltd [2000] EWCA Civ 348 (an elastic strap that sprang back into a child's eye) it failed because the risk was discoverable without any advance in knowledge.
- (f) for component producers, the defect is in the finished product and is attributable to its design or to the producer's instructions.
Contributory negligence also applies (s 6(4)).

Damage (s 5)
- Death, personal injury, or loss of or damage to property, including land.
- Not damage to the product itself or to a product supplied with it as a component (s 5(2)).
- Property must be of a kind ordinarily intended for private use and intended by the claimant mainly for private use (s 5(3)).
- No property claim unless it exceeds £275 (s 5(4)).

Limitation
Under the Limitation Act 1980 s 11A, claims must be brought within three years of the damage or of the claimant's date of knowledge, and in any event within ten years of the product being put into circulation (a long-stop).

Exam tips: run both routes, CPA (strict but limited by ss 4–5) and negligence (fault-based but covering business property and small claims), and identify every defendant in the supply chain.

The faculty describes trespass to the person as the civil counterpart of criminal assault. It covers three torts: battery, assault and false imprisonment. They are actionable per se (without proof of damage) and require direct interference. Since Letang v Cooper [1965] 1 QB 232 (CA), trespass is confined to intentional (or at least deliberate) conduct; unintended direct injury is a matter for negligence.

Battery
The intentional and direct application of unlawful force to another person.
- Any touching can suffice. Collins v Wilcock [1984] 1 WLR 1172: a police officer who held a woman's arm to detain her, without arresting her, committed battery. Touching within the generally acceptable conduct of everyday life (jostling in a crowd, a tap on the shoulder to attract attention) is not battery.
- Hostility: Wilson v Pringle [1987] QB 237 (CA) suggested the touching must be 'hostile'. In F v West Berkshire HA [1990] 2 AC 1 Lord Goff doubted any requirement of hostility, preferring the Collins v Wilcock approach.

Assault
Intentionally causing another to reasonably apprehend the immediate infliction of a battery.
- No contact is needed.
- Immediacy: Thomas v National Union of Mineworkers (South Wales Area) [1986] Ch 20: threats shouted by pickets at working miners being driven past in vehicles under police protection were not assault, as the pickets could not immediately carry them out.
- Words can negate a threat: Tuberville v Savage (1669) 1 Mod Rep 3, 'If it were not assize-time, I would not take such language from you', with a hand on a sword.

False imprisonment
The unlawful imposition of total restraint on another's freedom of movement.
- Total restraint: Bird v Jones (1845) 7 QB 742; blocking one route while another is open is not imprisonment.
- Knowledge is not required: Meering v Grahame-White Aviation Co (1919) 122 LT 44 (CA), approved obiter by Lord Griffiths in Murray v Ministry of Defence [1988] 1 WLR 692 (HL), where the claimant did know she was detained. But someone unaware of detention who suffers no harm may get only nominal damages.
- Reasonable conditions on leaving are allowed: Robertson v Balmain New Ferry Co Ltd [1910] AC 295 (PC), a penny charge to exit a wharf (the case is often miscited as Robinson v Balmain).
- Lawful authority is a complete answer, but where detention is unlawful because of a public law error, it is false imprisonment even if the person could lawfully have been detained. R (Lumba) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2011] UKSC 12 awarded only nominal damages on that basis.

Defences
- Consent: valid consent to the nature of the act is a defence. In medical cases, consent 'in broad terms' to the nature of the procedure defeats battery; failure to explain risks is a matter for negligence (Chatterton v Gerson [1981] QB 432; Montgomery).
- Necessity: treatment of an adult lacking capacity in their best interests (F v West Berkshire HA; now the Mental Capacity Act 2005 ss 5–6).
- Self-defence: in tort the defendant must have honestly and reasonably believed force was necessary, and the force must be reasonable: Ashley v Chief Constable of Sussex Police [2008] UKHL 25.
- Lawful arrest, e.g. under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 s 24.
- Contributory negligence is not a defence to an intentional battery: Co-operative Group (CWS) Ltd v Pritchard [2011] EWCA Civ 329.

Intentional infliction of harm: Wilkinson v Downton
Wilkinson v Downton [1897] 2 QB 57: a false practical joke that the claimant's husband had been badly injured caused her serious illness. Rhodes v OPO [2015] UKSC 32 restated the tort as having three elements:
- a conduct element: words or conduct directed at the claimant for which there is no justification or excuse;
- a mental element: an intention to cause physical harm or severe mental or emotional distress;
- a consequence element: physical harm or a recognised psychiatric illness.
There is no general tort of invasion of privacy at common law: Wainwright v Home Office [2003] UKHL 53. Harassment is covered by the Protection from Harassment Act 1997, which provides a civil remedy (s 3).

Exam tips: separate the three torts and apply each element. Consider consent and self-defence early, and remember trespass is actionable per se.

The faculty describes this topic as how the law allocates liability when two or more people commit the same wrong. It has two sides: the claimant's rights against several wrongdoers, and the wrongdoers' rights against each other.

Joint and several concurrent tortfeasors
- Joint tortfeasors commit the same tort together. Typical cases are employer and employee where the employer is vicariously liable, principal and agent, and persons acting in pursuance of a common design.
- Several concurrent tortfeasors commit separate torts that cause the same damage, e.g. two drivers who collide and injure a pedestrian: The Koursk [1924] P 140.
In both cases each defendant is liable to the claimant for the whole of the damage (liability 'in solidum'). The claimant may recover the full amount from any one of them, though not more than the total loss. The risk that one wrongdoer is insolvent therefore falls on the other wrongdoers, not on the claimant.

Accessory liability: common design
Fish & Fish Ltd v Sea Shepherd UK [2015] UKSC 10 set out when someone is jointly liable as an accessory to another's tort. The defendant must have:
- assisted the commission of the tort by the primary tortfeasor;
- done so pursuant to a common design with that tortfeasor that the tortious act be done;
- given assistance that is more than trivial or de minimis.
On the facts, a majority held the UK charity's involvement (passing on about £1,730 in donations raised for the campaign) was too minimal to make it jointly liable for damage done by its US-based parent's ship.

Successive actions and settlements
- At common law, judgment against one joint tortfeasor barred action against the others: Brinsmead v Harrison (1872). That rule was abolished by statute (now the Civil Liability (Contribution) Act 1978 s 3), so judgment against one is no bar to an action against another liable for the same damage.
- Jameson v Central Electricity Generating Board [2000] 1 AC 455: where a claimant accepts a settlement from one tortfeasor in full satisfaction of the claim, the claim against other concurrent tortfeasors for the same damage is extinguished.

Contribution between wrongdoers
The Civil Liability (Contribution) Act 1978 governs claims between defendants.
- s 1(1): a person liable in respect of any damage may recover contribution from any other person liable in respect of the same damage, whether jointly with him or otherwise, and whether the liability is in tort, contract, trust or otherwise (s 6(1)).
- 'Same damage' is construed strictly: Royal Brompton Hospital NHS Trust v Hammond [2002] UKHL 14.
- s 1(4): a defendant who settles bona fide may claim contribution without proving liability, provided he would have been liable had the factual basis of the claim been established.
- s 2(1): the amount is what the court finds just and equitable having regard to the extent of each person's responsibility for the damage. This involves both causative potency and relative blameworthiness.
- s 2(2): the court may exempt a person from contribution, or order a complete indemnity.
- s 2(3): a person cannot be ordered to contribute more than he would have had to pay the claimant (e.g. because of an exclusion clause or contributory negligence).
- Limitation: a contribution claim must be brought within two years of the judgment or settlement giving rise to it (Limitation Act 1980 s 10).

Contributory negligence alongside contribution
Fitzgerald v Lane [1989] AC 328 (HL): where a claimant is partly to blame and there are several defendants, the court first assesses the claimant's share against the defendants as a whole, then apportions the defendants' combined share between them under the 1978 Act. The two exercises must be kept separate.

Worked example
C suffers loss of £100,000. D1 and D2 are both liable for the same damage. The court finds C 20% contributorily negligent, so C recovers £80,000 and may enforce it against either defendant. If D1 pays the full £80,000 and the court apportions responsibility between the defendants 75:25, D1 can recover £20,000 from D2.

Exam tips: check the defendants caused the same damage (otherwise each is liable only for his own part), and calculate contributory negligence before contribution.

Vicarious liability makes one person (usually an employer) liable for a tort committed by another, without any fault of its own. The employee remains personally liable too.

The two-stage test
The Supreme Court has repeatedly restated a two-stage inquiry, most recently in Trustees of the Barry Congregation of Jehovah's Witnesses v BXB [2023] UKSC 15:
1. Is the relationship between the defendant and the tortfeasor one of employment, or 'akin to employment'?
2. Is the tort sufficiently closely connected with that relationship (and the tortfeasor's acts authorised by it) that it is fair and just to hold the defendant liable?

Stage 1: the relationship
- Employment is the paradigm.
- Various Claimants v Catholic Child Welfare Society [2012] UKSC 56 (the Christian Brothers case) extended liability to relationships akin to employment, and listed policy features: the defendant is more likely to be able to pay (often insured); the tort results from activity undertaken on the defendant's behalf; that activity is part of the defendant's business; by employing the tortfeasor the defendant created the risk; and the tortfeasor is to some degree under the defendant's control.
- Cox v Ministry of Justice [2016] UKSC 10: the prison service was vicariously liable for a prisoner working in the kitchen who injured the catering manager.
- Armes v Nottinghamshire CC [2017] UKSC 60: a local authority was vicariously liable for abuse by foster parents with whom it had placed a child.
- Barclays Bank plc v Various Claimants [2020] UKSC 13: a bank was not liable for a doctor who examined prospective employees, because he carried on his own independent business. The policy features are a guide, not separate tests.
- BXB [2023]: a congregation of Jehovah's Witnesses was in a relationship akin to employment with an elder.

Stage 2: close connection
- The older Salmond formula asked whether the act was an unauthorised mode of doing an authorised act. Compare Limpus v London General Omnibus Co (1862) 1 H & C 526 (racing a rival bus against orders: liable), Rose v Plenty [1976] 1 WLR 141 (milkman's prohibited child helper: liable) and Joel v Morison (1834) 6 C & P 501 (a 'frolic of his own': not liable).
- Lister v Hesley Hall Ltd [2001] UKHL 22 adopted a close connection test: a boarding-house warden's sexual abuse of boys in his care was so closely connected with his duties that the employer was liable.
- Dubai Aluminium Co Ltd v Salaam [2002] UKHL 48: the wrongful conduct must be so closely connected with acts the employee was authorised to do that it may fairly and properly be regarded as done in the ordinary course of employment.
- Mohamud v WM Morrison Supermarkets plc [2016] UKSC 11: a petrol kiosk attendant who followed a customer out and assaulted him made the employer liable; his job involved dealing with customers and the attack was an unbroken sequence of events.
- WM Morrison Supermarkets plc v Various Claimants [2020] UKSC 12: an employee who leaked colleagues' payroll data online to harm the employer was pursuing a personal vendetta, not acting in the course of employment, so Morrisons was not liable. Lord Reed stressed that Mohamud had not changed the Dubai Aluminium test.
- BXB [2023]: the elder's rape of a congregant was not sufficiently closely connected with his role as elder (it arose from a family friendship), so the congregation was not liable.

Related rules
- Dual vicarious liability is possible (Viasystems v Thermal Transfer [2005] EWCA Civ 1151), and the employer may in principle claim an indemnity from the employee (Lister v Romford Ice [1957] AC 555).
- Non-delegable duties are different: the defendant is liable for its own breach of a personal duty even if performance was delegated to an independent contractor. Woodland v Essex CC [2013] UKSC 66 (a school pupil injured during a swimming lesson run by a contractor) identified the features of such duties.

Justifications include enterprise risk, loss spreading through insurance and deterrence; critics say the expanded tests are uncertain.

Exam tips: always address both stages separately with cases. For abuse cases, compare Lister and Armes with BXB; for violent or vindictive employees, compare Mohamud with Morrison (2020).

cards.b: Duty of care, breach of that duty, damage caused by the breach, and damage not too remote; subject to defences.
Manufacturer owed a duty to the ultimate consumer; Lord Atkin's neighbour principle based on reasonable foreseeability and close and direct relationship.

cards.f: Caparo Industries plc v Dickman [1990] 2 AC 605
cards.b: Auditors owed no duty to investors; emphasised foreseeability, proximity, fair, just and reasonable, and incremental development.

cards.f: Robinson v CC West Yorkshire Police [2018] UKSC 4
cards.b: Caparo is not a universal three-stage test: apply established categories; in novel cases develop the law incrementally by analogy. Police owed duty to pedestrian injured during arrest.
No general duty to prevent harm or protect others from third parties (Smith v Littlewoods [1987] AC 241), subject to exceptions such as assumption of responsibility, control, or creating the danger.

cards.f: Home Office v Dorset Yacht Co [1970] AC 1004
cards.b: Borstal officers owed a duty to boat owners for damage by trainees who escaped through the officers' carelessness: control over the third parties.

cards.f: Michael v CC South Wales Police [2015] UKSC 2
cards.b: No duty to a 999 caller later killed by her ex-partner: no assumption of responsibility; police not liable for failing to protect from a third party.

cards.f: Tindall v CC Thames Valley Police [2024] UKSC 33
cards.b: Police who attended an icy road and left without making it safe owed no duty to a motorist later killed: they had not made matters worse.
A claimant within the range of foreseeable physical injury can recover for psychiatric injury even if psychiatric injury itself was not foreseeable.

Close tie of love and affection; proximity in time and space to the accident or its immediate aftermath; perception by own unaided senses; foreseeable psychiatric injury in a person of reasonable fortitude.
Mother who saw her injured family at hospital about two hours after the crash recovered: within the immediate aftermath.

cards.f: Paul v Royal Wolverhampton NHS Trust [2024] UKSC 1
cards.b: No secondary-victim recovery for witnessing a relative's death or medical crisis caused by earlier negligent failure to diagnose; recovery requires an accident or its immediate aftermath.
Financial loss not consequential on physical damage to the claimant's person or property; generally not recoverable for negligent acts.

cards.f: Spartan Steel v Martin & Co [1973] QB 27
cards.b: Power cut by negligent contractors: damage to the melt and its lost profit recoverable; lost profits on further melts were pure economic loss and not recoverable.
A duty can arise for negligent misstatements causing economic loss where there is a special relationship and assumption of responsibility; the disclaimer defeated the claim on the facts.
Extended assumption of responsibility to the provision of services, and allowed concurrent liability in contract and tort.
Negligence is omitting to do what a reasonable person would do, or doing what a prudent and reasonable person would not do.
A learner driver is held to the standard of a reasonably competent driver; the standard is objective.
Cricket ball injuring a passer-by: the risk was so small that a reasonable person could disregard it, so no breach.
Employer should have provided goggles to a one-eyed worker because the consequences of injury were especially serious.
After a flood, sawdust on the floor was reasonable; closing the factory would have been disproportionate to the risk.
A professional is not negligent if acting in accordance with a practice accepted as proper by a responsible body of opinion in that field (Bolam [1957] 1 WLR 582).

cards.f: Bolitho v City and Hackney HA [1998] AC 232
cards.b: Professional opinion relied on under Bolam must have a logical basis and withstand analysis.
Doctors must take reasonable care to ensure patients know of material risks and reasonable alternatives; materiality judged by the reasonable patient or this patient.

cards.f: Barnett v Chelsea & Kensington HMC [1969] 1 QB 428
cards.b: Negligent failure to examine was not a cause of death because the patient would have died from arsenic poisoning anyway: 'but for' test.
Defendant liable where its breach made a material (more than minimal) contribution to the claimant's disease.
Mesothelioma: each negligent employer that materially increased the risk was liable despite inability to prove which exposure caused the disease.
Reversed Barker v Corus for mesothelioma: defendants liable under Fairchild are jointly and severally liable for the whole damage.
Rejected Re Polemis: a defendant is liable only for damage of a reasonably foreseeable kind.
The precise manner of harm need not be foreseeable if the type of harm (burns) was foreseeable.
If harm of a foreseeable type occurs, the defendant takes the claimant as found and is liable for its full extent (Smith v Leech Brain [1962] 2 QB 405).
Damages reduced to the extent the court thinks just and equitable having regard to the claimant's share in responsibility for the damage.
Anyone with a sufficient degree of control over premises; there may be more than one occupier.
To take such care as in all the circumstances is reasonable to see that the visitor will be reasonably safe in using the premises for the permitted purposes.
Occupier must be prepared for children to be less careful than adults (e.g. Glasgow Corp v Taylor; but Phipps v Rochester: parents expected to supervise very young children).

cards.f: OLA 1957 s 2(3)(b) and Roles v Nathan
cards.b: Occupier may expect a person exercising a calling to guard against its ordinary risks; chimney sweeps killed by fumes they were warned about could not recover.
Not liable for an independent contractor's faulty work if reasonable to entrust it, and reasonable steps taken to check competence and, where appropriate, the work.

Duty to non-visitor if occupier knows or has reasonable grounds to believe of (a) the danger and (b) the entrant's presence nearby, and (c) the risk is one he may reasonably be expected to protect against.
No liability to non-visitors under the 1984 Act for loss of or damage to property.
No liability for injury from diving into a shallow lake: risk was obvious, arose from the claimant's free choice rather than the state of premises, and prevention would destroy a public amenity.

cards.f: Hunter v Canary Wharf Ltd [1997] AC 655
cards.b: Only those with a proprietary interest or exclusive possession can sue in private nuisance; blocking TV reception by a building was not actionable.
Character of the neighbourhood matters to amenity nuisance; coming to the nuisance is no defence; 20 years' prescription runs only while the nuisance is actionable.

cards.f: St Helen's Smelting Co v Tipping (1865)
cards.b: Where a nuisance causes material physical damage to property, the character of the locality is irrelevant.
A malicious motive can make otherwise reasonable conduct a nuisance: Christie v Davey [1893] (banging on the wall); Hollywood Silver Fox Farm v Emmett [1936] (guns fired to disturb foxes).
Constant viewing into neighbouring flats from a public viewing platform was a nuisance: not a common and ordinary use of land and a substantial interference.
Coming to the nuisance no defence; planning permission not a defence in itself; courts have a wider discretion than Shelfer suggested to award damages instead of an injunction.
An occupier who knows of a nuisance created by a trespasser and continues or adopts it (here a blocked pipe) is liable.

cards.f: Cambridge Water v Eastern Counties Leather [1994] 2 AC 264
cards.b: Foreseeability of the relevant type of harm is required for damages in nuisance and in Rylands v Fletcher.

cards.f: Who is liable under CPA 1987 s 2(2)?
cards.b: The producer, an own-brander holding himself out as producer, and the person who imported the product into the UK in the course of business to supply it.
A supplier is liable if, on a timely request, it fails within a reasonable period to identify the producer/importer or its own supplier.
Safety not such as persons generally are entitled to expect, considering marketing, get-up, instructions and warnings, expected use, and time of supply.

cards.f: A v National Blood Authority [2001] 3 All ER 289
cards.b: Hepatitis-C infected blood was defective: the public was entitled to expect it to be free of infection; unavoidability of the risk was irrelevant; development risks defence failed.
The state of scientific and technical knowledge at the relevant time did not enable a producer of similar products to discover the defect.
Favoured a flexible, holistic approach to 'defect' that may weigh risks, benefits and avoidability, departing from aspects of the approach in A v NBA.
Damage to the product itself or a product containing it; property not for private use; property claims of £275 or less.
Three years from damage or date of knowledge (Limitation Act 1980 s 11A), with a ten-year long-stop from when the product was put into circulation.
Intentional and direct application of unlawful force to another; actionable per se. Touching within everyday acceptable conduct is excluded (Collins v Wilcock [1984]).
Intentionally causing another to reasonably apprehend the immediate infliction of a battery; no contact needed.
Unlawful imposition of total restraint on another's freedom of movement; no need for the claimant to know (Meering (1919), approved obiter in Murray v MoD [1988]).
Unintentional direct injury lies in negligence, not trespass; trespass to the person requires intentional conduct.

cards.f: Thomas v NUM (South Wales Area) [1986] Ch 20
cards.b: Pickets shouting threats at miners in vehicles protected by police: no assault because the threatened violence could not be immediately carried out.
Blocking one route while leaving the claimant free to go another way is not false imprisonment: restraint must be total.

cards.f: Ashley v CC Sussex Police [2008] UKHL 25
cards.b: Civil self-defence requires an honest and reasonable belief that force was necessary (stricter than the criminal test).
Wilkinson v Downton tort: unjustified words/conduct directed at C, intention to cause physical harm or severe distress, causing physical harm or recognised psychiatric illness.
Joint: same tort committed together (vicarious liability, agency, common design). Several concurrent: separate torts causing the same damage. Both are each liable in full to C.

cards.f: Fish & Fish v Sea Shepherd UK [2015] UKSC 10
cards.b: Accessory liability needs assistance in the primary tort, pursuant to a common design, which is more than de minimis; the UK charity's minimal role did not suffice.
Anyone liable for any damage may recover contribution from any other person liable for the same damage, whether jointly or otherwise.
Contribution is what is just and equitable having regard to the extent of each person's responsibility for the damage.
The court may exempt a person from contribution or order a complete indemnity.
A settlement with one concurrent tortfeasor accepted in full satisfaction extinguishes the claim against others for the same damage.
First assess the claimant's contributory negligence against all defendants together, then apportion the defendants' share between them.
Two years from the judgment or settlement giving rise to the right (Limitation Act 1980 s 10).
(1) Relationship of employment or akin to employment; (2) the tort is sufficiently closely connected with that relationship to make it fair and just to impose liability (BXB [2023] UKSC 15).

cards.f: Various Claimants v Catholic Child Welfare Society [2012] UKSC 56
cards.b: Vicarious liability extends to relationships akin to employment; five policy features including ability to pay, activity on D's behalf, part of D's business, creation of risk, control.

cards.f: Barclays Bank v Various Claimants [2020] UKSC 13
cards.b: Bank not liable for a self-employed doctor carrying on his own independent business: not akin to employment.
Close connection test: employer liable for warden's sexual abuse of boys in his care because it was closely connected with his duties.

cards.f: Mohamud v WM Morrison Supermarkets [2016] UKSC 11
cards.b: Employer liable for kiosk attendant's assault on a customer: within his field of activities and an unbroken sequence of events.

cards.f: WM Morrison Supermarkets v Various Claimants [2020] UKSC 12
cards.b: No liability for an employee who leaked staff data to harm the employer: a personal vendetta, not in the course of employment.
Elder was in a relationship akin to employment, but his rape of a congregant was not closely connected to his role, so no vicarious liability.
The education authority owed a non-delegable duty to a pupil injured in a swimming lesson run by an independent contractor: liability for its own breach, not vicarious.

questions.q: According to Robinson v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire Police [2018] UKSC 4, how should a court approach the existence of a duty in a case within an established category, such as a driver injuring a pedestrian?
options: Apply the established law without re-examining policy
Apply the three-stage Caparo test afresh
Apply the two-stage Anns test
Ask whether the defendant assumed responsibility
questions.why: Robinson holds that in established categories the court applies existing principles; the Caparo factors are relevant mainly to novel situations. Anns was overruled in Murphy v Brentwood. Assumption of responsibility is relevant to omissions and economic loss, not to an ordinary driving case.

questions.q: D, a security company, notices a fire starting in an empty neighbouring building it has no connection with and does nothing; the fire spreads to C's house. What is the most likely position?
options: D is liable because the damage was foreseeable
D is not liable because it is a pure omission with no recognised exception
D is liable because it is a business
D is liable because nuisance replaces negligence here
questions.why: Foreseeability alone does not create a duty to act: Smith v Littlewoods. D did not create the danger, control the land or the fire-starter, or assume responsibility to C, so no exception applies. Being a business does not create a duty to rescue, and nuisance would need D to be the occupier or creator of the state of affairs.

questions.q: Explain the distinction between acts and omissions in the law of negligence, with reference to at least two decided cases.
markScheme: States the general rule: no duty to prevent harm or confer a benefit (Smith v Littlewoods)
Explains the rationale (individual autonomy, 'why pick on me', burden of positive duties)
Identifies exceptions: assumption of responsibility, control of third party (Dorset Yacht), creation of danger, control of land
Applies the distinction to public authorities/police (Michael, Robinson, Tindall or N v Poole)
Notes that making matters worse is treated as an act
questions.modelAnswer: English law distinguishes harming someone (an act, which attracts ordinary negligence liability) from failing to protect them or to confer a benefit (an omission), for which there is generally no duty: Smith v Littlewoods Organisation Ltd [1987] AC 241, where a cinema owner was not liable for a fire started by trespassers in its empty building. The rationale is that positive duties restrict liberty and it is hard to say why one bystander rather than another should act. There are exceptions: where the defendant assumed responsibility to the claimant; where it controlled the third party (Home Office v Dorset Yacht [1970] AC 1004); where it created the danger; or where it controlled the land or thing from which the danger came. The distinction is central to cases against the police: in Michael [2015] UKSC 2 there was no duty to protect a victim from a third party, while in Robinson [2018] UKSC 4 officers who themselves created the danger during an arrest were liable, and in Tindall [2024] UKSC 33 officers who did not make an icy road more dangerous owed no duty.

questions.q: C's brother is crushed in a stadium crush caused by D's negligence. C watches events live on television at home and develops PTSD. Applying Alcock, why is C's claim likely to fail?
options: PTSD is not a recognised psychiatric illness
C did not perceive the event with his own unaided senses and lacked proximity
C was a primary victim
Siblings can never recover
questions.why: In Alcock watching live television did not satisfy the requirement of perception by one's own senses, and C was not present at the scene or its immediate aftermath. Siblings can recover if they prove a close tie (it is just not presumed). PTSD is a recognised psychiatric illness. C was never in physical danger, so he is not a primary victim.

questions.q: Contractors negligently cut a power cable supplying C's factory, which loses a day's production. No property of C is damaged. Which best describes C's position?
options: C recovers all lost profits as consequential loss
C can recover under Hedley Byrne because it relied on the supply
C can recover only if the contractors were public authorities
C's loss is pure economic loss and generally irrecoverable
questions.why: With no physical damage to C's property, lost production is pure economic loss: Spartan Steel. Hedley Byrne requires an assumption of responsibility, typically through advice or services, not mere dependence on a utility. The status of the defendant is irrelevant to this rule.

questions.q: Explain how the courts have controlled liability for pure economic loss caused by negligent misstatements.
markScheme: States the general exclusionary rule for pure economic loss (Spartan Steel / Murphy)
Hedley Byrne: special relationship, reliance, assumption of responsibility
Caparo: purpose of statement and known recipient; no duty to the public at large
Extensions: Henderson v Merrett (services), White v Jones, Spring v Guardian, Smith v Eric S Bush
Limits: Williams v Natural Life (personal assumption), Customs & Excise v Barclays
Disclaimers controlled by UCTA 1977 / Consumer Rights Act 2015
questions.modelAnswer: Pure economic loss caused by negligent acts is generally irrecoverable (Spartan Steel [1973]; Murphy v Brentwood [1991]). Hedley Byrne v Heller [1964] created an exception for statements: where the defendant, possessing special skill, assumes responsibility to the claimant who reasonably relies on the statement, a duty arises, though there the disclaimer defeated the claim. Caparo [1990] confines the duty: the maker must know the statement will be communicated to the claimant, specifically or as one of an identifiable class, for a particular transaction, and that the claimant will rely on it; auditors' statutory accounts did not ground a duty to investors. Henderson v Merrett [1995] extended the principle to services, and White v Jones [1995] and Spring v Guardian [1995] recognised duties to disappointed beneficiaries and to the subject of a reference. The courts police the boundary through assumption of responsibility: no personal liability for a director without a personal assumption (Williams v Natural Life [1998]) and no duty from a bank merely notified of a freezing order (Customs and Excise v Barclays [2006]). Disclaimers can negate assumption of responsibility but must satisfy UCTA 1977 (Smith v Eric S Bush [1990]) or, for consumers, the Consumer Rights Act 2015.

questions.q: A 17-year-old learner driver, on her second lesson, mounts the pavement and injures a pedestrian. Which standard of care applies?
options: That of a professional driving instructor
That of a reasonably competent driver
That of a reasonable learner on her second lesson
That of a reasonable 17-year-old
questions.why: Nettleship v Weston: the standard is objective, that of the reasonably competent driver, regardless of inexperience. The age-adjusted standard in Mullin v Richards applies to children's ordinary activities, not to driving on the road. A professional instructor standard would be too high.

questions.q: Which case establishes that a doctor's advice about the risks of treatment is NOT governed by the Bolam test?
options: Wilsher v Essex AHA
Bolitho v City and Hackney HA
Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board
Roe v Minister of Health
questions.why: Montgomery [2015] UKSC 11 replaced Bolam for the disclosure of material risks with a patient-focused test. Bolitho qualified Bolam for treatment decisions; Roe concerns judging by knowledge at the time; Wilsher is a causation case.

questions.q: Explain how the courts decide whether a defendant has breached the duty of care, using decided cases.
markScheme: Objective reasonable person standard (Blyth; Nettleship)
Likelihood of harm (Bolton v Stone)
Seriousness of harm (Paris v Stepney)
Cost/practicability of precautions (Latimer) and social utility (Watt; Compensation Act 2006 s 1; SARAH 2015)
Special standards: professionals (Bolam/Bolitho) or children (Mullin)
questions.modelAnswer: Breach asks whether the defendant fell below the standard of the reasonable person (Blyth v Birmingham Waterworks), an objective standard that ignores personal inexperience (Nettleship v Weston). The court weighs factors. The more likely the harm, the more care is required; in Bolton v Stone a very small risk of a cricket ball escaping could be ignored. The graver the potential harm, the greater the precautions; in Paris v Stepney a one-eyed worker should have had goggles. Against these the court sets the cost and practicability of precautions (Latimer v AEC: no need to close the factory) and the social value of the activity (Watt v Hertfordshire; Compensation Act 2006 s 1; Social Action, Responsibility and Heroism Act 2015). The standard is adjusted for certain defendants: professionals are judged by responsible professional practice (Bolam), provided it is logically defensible (Bolitho), while children are judged against a reasonable child of the same age (Mullin v Richards).

questions.q: D negligently spills oil into a harbour. It is not reasonably foreseeable that the oil could ignite on water, but it does, destroying C's wharf. Applying The Wagon Mound (No 1), D is:
options: Liable, because the damage was a direct consequence
Liable, under the eggshell skull rule
Not liable, because damage by fire was not a reasonably foreseeable kind of damage
Not liable, because there was no duty of care
questions.why: The Wagon Mound (No 1) replaced the Re Polemis directness test with foreseeability of the kind of damage; fire damage was not foreseeable. The eggshell skull rule applies only once harm of a foreseeable type has occurred. The issue is remoteness, not duty.

questions.q: Which case refused recovery where negligent delay in diagnosis reduced the claimant's chance of avoiding a bad outcome from 25% to nil?
options: Sienkiewicz v Greif
Hotson v East Berkshire AHA
Chester v Afshar
McGhee v NCB
questions.why: In Hotson the claimant had only a 25% chance of a good outcome even with prompt treatment, so on the balance of probabilities the delay did not cause the disability, and a lost chance was not compensable. Chester relaxed causation for failure to warn; McGhee and Sienkiewicz concern material increase in risk.

questions.q: When will a later act of the claimant or a third party break the chain of causation? Refer to decided cases.
markScheme: Explains novus actus as a question of whether the later act is a fresh independent cause
Third parties: negligent/deliberate acts may break chain if independent and not within the risk (Knightley v Johns)
Claimant: unreasonable conduct may break chain (McKew)
Contrast Corr v IBC: suicide caused by the depression from the accident does not break the chain
Notes that foreseeable interventions within the risk created do not break the chain (Dorset Yacht style reasoning)
questions.modelAnswer: A novus actus interveniens is a later event so independent and potent that the defendant's breach is no longer treated as a legal cause of the damage. For third parties, the more foreseeable the intervention, and the more it falls within the very risk the defendant's carelessness created, the less likely it is to break the chain. In Knightley v Johns the negligent order of a police inspector, after a crash in a tunnel, sending an officer the wrong way through traffic broke the chain from the original driver's negligence. A claimant's own conduct breaks the chain only if wholly unreasonable: in McKew v Holland & Hannen & Cubitts, a man with an injured leg who went down steep stairs without a handrail or assistance broke the chain. By contrast, in Corr v IBC Vehicles, a worker's suicide resulting from depression caused by the accident did not break the chain, because it was not a free and informed choice independent of the defendant's breach. Lesser fault on the claimant's part is dealt with by contributory negligence instead.

questions.q: A professional electrician is electrocuted while repairing faulty wiring in D's office after D told him the circuit was live. Which provision is most directly relevant to D's defence?
questions.why: s 2(3)(b) lets an occupier expect a person in the exercise of his calling to guard against risks ordinarily incident to it (Roles v Nathan). s 2(3)(a) concerns children; s 1(8) of the 1984 Act concerns property damage to non-visitors; s 2(4)(b) concerns the occupier's liability for work done by independent contractors.

questions.q: C, an adult trespasser, climbs a fence at night and dives into a disused quarry pool, hitting a submerged rock. The owner knew people sometimes swam there and had put up 'Danger: no swimming' signs. What is the most likely outcome?
options: Liability under OLA 1957 because C was on the land
No liability: the risk was obvious, voluntarily run, and warnings were given
Liability under OLA 1984 because the owner knew of trespassers
Liability for C's damaged clothing under OLA 1984
questions.why: C is a trespasser, so only the 1984 Act applies. Even if s 1(3) is satisfied, warnings can discharge the duty (s 1(5)), there is no duty for risks willingly accepted (s 1(6)), and Tomlinson and Ratcliff deny liability for obvious risks run by choice. The 1957 Act protects visitors only, and s 1(8) excludes property damage.

questions.q: Compare the duties owed by an occupier to visitors and to trespassers in England and Wales.
markScheme: Visitors: OLA 1957 common duty of care s 2(1)-(2)
Relevant circumstances s 2(3) (children; persons exercising a calling), warnings s 2(4)(a), contractors s 2(4)(b)
Trespassers: OLA 1984 duty arises only if s 1(3)(a)-(c) satisfied
1984 duty content s 1(4), discharged by warning s 1(5), no property damage s 1(8)
Both: no liability for willingly accepted/obvious risks (s 2(5), s 1(6); Tomlinson)
questions.modelAnswer: Under the OLA 1957 an occupier owes every visitor the common duty of care (s 2(1)): to take reasonable care to see that the visitor is reasonably safe in using the premises for the permitted purposes (s 2(2)). The circumstances include that children are less careful (s 2(3)(a)) and that skilled visitors can guard against the risks of their calling (s 2(3)(b)). A warning suffices only if it enables the visitor to be reasonably safe (s 2(4)(a)), and work by competent, reasonably checked contractors does not render the occupier liable (s 2(4)(b)). Under the OLA 1984 a duty to a trespasser arises only if the occupier knows or has reasonable grounds to believe in the danger and in the entrant's likely presence, and the risk is one against which some protection may reasonably be expected (s 1(3)). The duty is to take reasonable care to see that the entrant is not injured by the danger (s 1(4)); it may be discharged by warnings or discouragement (s 1(5)) and does not cover property damage (s 1(8)). Under both Acts there is no duty for risks willingly accepted (s 2(5); s 1(6)), and obvious risks freely run will usually defeat a claim (Tomlinson v Congleton BC).

questions.q: C's adult son lives with C in the house C owns. Both are disturbed by D's late-night industrial noise. Who can sue D in private nuisance?
options: Both C and the son
Only C
Only the son, as he is the more affected
Neither, because noise is not a nuisance
questions.why: Hunter v Canary Wharf requires a proprietary interest or exclusive possession, which C has as owner and the son lacks. Noise is a classic amenity nuisance, so the last option is wrong.

questions.q: D's factory has caused physical damage to C's crops through emissions. D argues the area is industrial. Which case shows this argument fails?
options: Leakey v National Trust
St Helen's Smelting Co v Tipping
Sturges v Bridgman
Hunter v Canary Wharf
questions.why: St Helen's Smelting held that locality is irrelevant where there is material physical damage to property. Sturges v Bridgman made locality relevant to amenity nuisance; Hunter concerns standing; Leakey concerns natural hazards and the measured duty.

questions.q: Is it a defence to a claim in private nuisance that the claimant 'came to the nuisance' or that the defendant has planning permission? Discuss.
markScheme: Coming to the nuisance is no defence: Sturges v Bridgman; Miller v Jackson; Coventry v Lawrence
Explains rationale: nuisance protects land, not particular owners; otherwise defendant could acquire right without 20 years' prescription
Planning permission not a defence in itself (Coventry v Lawrence)
May be relevant to character of locality where it changes the area, and to remedy
Mentions statutory authority as a true defence by contrast (Allen v Gulf Oil)
questions.modelAnswer: Coming to the nuisance is not a defence. In Sturges v Bridgman a doctor who built a consulting room next to a confectioner's long-established noisy machinery succeeded; the confectioner could not rely on prescription because the interference only became actionable when the consulting room was built. The Court of Appeal in Miller v Jackson found a cricket club liable to new householders, though the majority refused an injunction, and the Supreme Court in Coventry v Lawrence confirmed the rule, while noting that a claimant's change of use of their own land might be relevant. Planning permission is likewise not a defence in itself: a planning authority cannot authorise a private wrong, so permission does not legalise a nuisance (Coventry v Lawrence). However, where permission is implemented and changes the character of the locality, that may affect what is reasonable, and the public interest reflected in it may influence the choice between an injunction and damages. This contrasts with statutory authority, which is a true defence where the nuisance is the inevitable result of what Parliament authorised (Allen v Gulf Oil).

questions.q: C buys a toaster which, because of a manufacturing fault, catches fire. It destroys itself and damages C's kitchen worktop (repair cost £900). Under the CPA 1987, C can recover:
options: The worktop only
Both the toaster and the worktop
The toaster only
Nothing, because there was no personal injury
questions.why: Under s 5(2) there is no liability for damage to the defective product itself, but damage to other private property above £275 is recoverable (s 5(3)-(4)). The CPA covers property damage, not only personal injury. The cost of the toaster could be claimed in contract from the seller.

questions.q: In Abouzaid v Mothercare (UK) Ltd, why did the development risks defence fail?
options: The defendant was not the producer
The risk could have been discovered without any advance in scientific or technical knowledge
The product complied with legal requirements
The claimant was contributorily negligent
questions.why: The danger of an elastic strap springing back could have been appreciated by a simple practical test; s 4(1)(e) protects only against defects undiscoverable given the state of scientific and technical knowledge. Mothercare's status as a defendant was not the issue on appeal, and neither compliance with legal requirements nor contributory negligence was the basis of the decision.

questions.q: Compare the claimant's position in negligence and under Part I of the Consumer Protection Act 1987 when injured by a defective product.
markScheme: Negligence: Donoghue duty; claimant must prove fault (Grant v Australian Knitting Mills: inference from defect)
CPA: strict liability for defect (s 2, s 3), no need to prove fault
CPA wider range of defendants (producer, own-brander, importer, supplier s 2(3))
CPA limits: s 4 defences especially development risks; s 5 damage restrictions (£275; private property; product itself)
Limitation: CPA s 11A 10-year long-stop vs ordinary negligence limitation
Conclusion: both routes often pleaded together
questions.modelAnswer: In negligence, the manufacturer owes the ultimate consumer a duty (Donoghue v Stevenson), but the claimant must prove a failure to take reasonable care, though a court may infer negligence from the nature of the defect (Grant v Australian Knitting Mills). Under the CPA 1987, liability is strict: the claimant must prove only that the product was defective in the s 3 sense, i.e. not as safe as persons generally are entitled to expect, and that the defect caused the damage. The CPA also widens the potential defendants to own-branders and UK importers (s 2(2)) and to suppliers who fail to identify their source (s 2(3)). On the other hand, the CPA has defences that negligence does not need in the same form, notably the development risks defence (s 4(1)(e)), interpreted narrowly in A v National Blood Authority. Its compensable damage is restricted: no claim for the product itself, for business property, or for property damage of £275 or less (s 5). It is subject to a ten-year long-stop from circulation (Limitation Act 1980 s 11A). Negligence therefore remains useful for business property, small claims and claims outside the long-stop, so claimants commonly plead both.

questions.q: D, a security guard, locks C in a storeroom for an hour while C is asleep inside; C never wakes and suffers no harm. Which statement is correct?
options: This is battery, not false imprisonment
False imprisonment is committed, but damages are likely to be nominal
There is no tort because no damage was caused
There is no tort because C did not know
questions.why: Meering, approved obiter by the House of Lords in Murray v Ministry of Defence, holds knowledge is not required; trespass is actionable per se, so lack of damage does not prevent liability but limits damages. There is no application of force, so it is not battery.

questions.q: A surgeon explains the nature of an operation to C, who consents, but does not mention a 1% risk of nerve damage, which materialises. C's best claim is in:
options: False imprisonment
Assault
Negligence, for failure to disclose a material risk
Battery, because consent was not informed
questions.why: Chatterton v Gerson: consent in broad terms to the nature of the procedure prevents battery; non-disclosure of risks is a matter for negligence, judged under Montgomery. False imprisonment and assault do not fit the facts.

questions.q: Explain the elements of the tort in Wilkinson v Downton as restated in Rhodes v OPO, and explain why the claim failed in Rhodes.
markScheme: Facts of Wilkinson v Downton (false statement causing illness)
Conduct element: words/conduct directed at C without justification or excuse
Mental element: intention to cause physical harm or severe mental or emotional distress
Consequence element: physical harm or recognised psychiatric illness
Rhodes: publication of the author's own life story had justification (freedom of expression; legitimate interest), and intention not shown; injunction discharged
questions.modelAnswer: In Wilkinson v Downton the defendant, as a practical joke, falsely told the claimant her husband had been seriously injured, and she suffered a serious illness; she recovered damages. In Rhodes v OPO the Supreme Court restated the tort with three elements. The conduct element requires words or conduct directed at the claimant for which there is no justification or reasonable excuse. The mental element requires an intention to cause physical harm or severe mental or emotional distress. The consequence element requires physical harm or a recognised psychiatric illness. In Rhodes, a musician's memoir describing the abuse he had suffered as a child could not be restrained at the suit of his vulnerable son. The publication of his own true story was justified, given the public interest and his freedom of expression, and the conduct element and intention were not established, so the interim injunction was discharged.

questions.q: Two negligent drivers, D1 and D2, collide and injure pedestrian C (who is blameless). D2 is uninsured and insolvent. How much can C recover from D1?
options: Half the damages
D1's share as apportioned by the court
Nothing until D2's insolvency is resolved
The full damages
questions.why: Concurrent tortfeasors causing the same damage are each liable in full to the claimant (The Koursk). Apportionment under the 1978 Act operates only between D1 and D2, so D1 bears the risk of D2's insolvency.
