questions.q: C suffers £60,000 loss caused by D1 and D2 and is found 1/3 contributorily negligent. The court apportions responsibility between D1 and D2 equally. D1 pays C in full. How much can D1 recover from D2?
questions.why: Following Fitzgerald v Lane, first reduce C's damages by 1/3: C recovers £40,000. D1 pays all £40,000 and can recover D2's half, £20,000. £30,000 ignores the contributory negligence; £40,000 is the whole award; £10,000 is half of the £20,000 deducted for C's contributory negligence, not half of the award.

questions.q: Explain how liability is allocated between two defendants who are both liable for the same damage, referring to the Civil Liability (Contribution) Act 1978.
markScheme: Each liable in full to claimant (in solidum); claimant cannot recover more than loss
s 1(1) right to contribution for same damage; any basis of liability
s 2(1) just and equitable, considering responsibility (causation and blameworthiness)
s 2(2) exemption/complete indemnity; s 2(3) cap at what defendant would have paid
s 1(4) settlements; two-year limitation (LA 1980 s 10); s 3 judgment no bar
questions.modelAnswer: As against the claimant, each defendant liable for the same damage is liable for the whole, and the claimant may choose whom to enforce against, though not recovering more than the total loss. Between the defendants, s 1(1) of the Civil Liability (Contribution) Act 1978 gives any person liable for damage a right to contribution from anyone else liable for the same damage, whatever the basis of their liability (tort, contract, trust or otherwise). By s 2(1) the amount is what is just and equitable having regard to each person's responsibility, which takes account of both causative potency and blameworthiness. The court may exempt a party or order a full indemnity (s 2(2)), but cannot order a party to pay more than it would have been liable to pay the claimant (s 2(3)). A party who settles in good faith may claim contribution if it would have been liable on the facts alleged (s 1(4)). Judgment against one wrongdoer is no bar to suing another (s 3), and a contribution claim must be brought within two years of the judgment or settlement (Limitation Act 1980 s 10).

questions.q: A bank arranges for a self-employed doctor, with his own practice, to examine job applicants. He assaults some of them. Following Barclays Bank v Various Claimants [2020] UKSC 13, the bank is:
options: Not vicariously liable because the doctor was carrying on his own independent business
Liable because it owed a non-delegable duty to the applicants
Vicariously liable because the examinations benefited the bank
Vicariously liable because sexual assault is always closely connected with medical examination
questions.why: The Supreme Court held the relationship was not akin to employment: the doctor ran his own business with many clients. Benefit to the defendant is only one factor. Close connection is irrelevant if stage 1 fails. The court did not find a non-delegable duty.

questions.q: Which case held an employer NOT vicariously liable because the employee was pursuing a personal vendetta against it?
options: WM Morrison Supermarkets v Various Claimants (2020)
Mohamud v WM Morrison Supermarkets (2016)
Lister v Hesley Hall (2001)
Rose v Plenty (1976)
questions.why: In the 2020 Morrison case an auditor leaked payroll data to damage his employer; this was not done in the course of employment. Mohamud (2016) found liability for an assault on a customer; Lister found liability for abuse by a warden; Rose v Plenty found liability for a milkman's prohibited use of a child helper.

questions.q: When will a defendant be vicariously liable for the tort of someone who is not its employee?
markScheme: Stage 1 extension: relationship akin to employment (CCWS 2012)
Policy features from CCWS, as guides not tests
Examples: Cox (prisoner), Armes (foster parents), BXB (elder)
Limit: independent contractor carrying on own business (Barclays 2020)
Still need stage 2 close connection
questions.modelAnswer: Vicarious liability is not confined to employment. Since Various Claimants v Catholic Child Welfare Society [2012] UKSC 56, it extends to relationships 'akin to employment'. Lord Phillips identified features making liability fair: the defendant is better placed to compensate, the tort arises from activity done on its behalf and integral to its business, it created the risk by engaging the tortfeasor, and it controls the tortfeasor to some degree. Applying this, the prison service was liable for a prisoner working in its kitchen (Cox v Ministry of Justice [2016]), a local authority for foster parents (Armes [2017]), and a congregation for an elder (BXB [2023]). But Barclays Bank v Various Claimants [2020] UKSC 13 held there is no liability for a true independent contractor carrying on his own business, and that the policy features are only a guide to whether the relationship is akin to employment. Even where stage 1 is met, the claimant must also show close connection, which failed in BXB.

questions.q: Ali, a delivery driver employed by Speedy Ltd, is running late and drives at 50 mph on a 30 mph residential road. He hits Ben, a cyclist, who suffers a broken leg. Ben was not wearing a helmet, but his head was not injured. Ben's mother, Cara, arrives at the hospital about an hour later, sees Ben in great pain before he is treated, and develops a recognised psychiatric illness. At the hospital, Dr Dee negligently fails to X-ray Ben's leg for two days; expert evidence is that, even with a prompt X-ray, there was a 40% chance Ben would have been left with a permanent limp, which he now has. Advise Ben and Cara on their claims in the tort of negligence. (Ignore any claims under the Human Rights Act.)
markScheme: Ben v Ali: established duty (road users); breach: speeding falls below reasonably competent driver standard (Nettleship; Blyth)
Speedy Ltd vicariously liable: employee, driving in course of employment despite breaking rules (Limpus; Dubai Aluminium)
Contributory negligence: no helmet but no head injury, so no causal contribution and no reduction (Froom v Butcher reasoning)
Ben v Dr Dee: established duty and breach (Bolam/Bolitho); causation of limp: 60% probability that delay caused it, so 'but for' satisfied on balance of probabilities (contrast Hotson, Gregg v Scott)

Ali/Speedy also liable for the limp unless Dee's negligence breaks chain (generally medical negligence not a novus actus unless grossly negligent; Knightley); same damage gives contribution under the 1978 Act
Cara: secondary victim; Alcock controls: close tie presumed for parent; immediate aftermath (McLoughlin: two hours at hospital); own senses; recognised illness
Paul [2024] UKSC 1: there was an accident (the collision), so the claim against Ali/Speedy may proceed; no claim against Dr Dee as a secondary victim of medical negligence
Conclusion with remedies and likely outcome
questions.modelAnswer:
Ben against Ali and Speedy Ltd. A driver owes other road users a duty of care; this is an established category, so following Robinson [2018] UKSC 4 no fresh Caparo analysis is needed. Driving at 50 mph in a 30 mph residential area falls below the standard of the reasonably competent driver (Blyth; Nettleship v Weston), so Ali is in breach. But for the speeding, the collision and broken leg would probably not have happened, and the injury is of a foreseeable type (The Wagon Mound (No 1)). Speedy Ltd is vicariously liable. Ali is an employee (stage 1), and driving to make deliveries, even in a forbidden manner, is a wrongful mode of doing what he was employed to do, so the tort is closely connected with his employment (Limpus v London General Omnibus; Dubai Aluminium v Salaam). Ben's failure to wear a helmet would be contributory negligence under the 1945 Act only if it contributed to his damage. As his head was not injured, there is no causal contribution and no reduction (compare Froom v Butcher).

Ben against Dr Dee (who owes him a duty as his doctor). Failing to X-ray a suspected fracture for two days is unlikely to be supported by a responsible body of medical opinion that withstands logical analysis (Bolam; Bolitho). On causation, even prompt treatment carried a 40% risk of a limp, so there was a 60% chance of avoiding it. On the balance of probabilities the delay caused the limp, and Ben recovers in full for it. Contrast Hotson and Gregg v Scott, where causation could not be proved on the balance of probabilities. The limp is also within the risk created by Ali's driving: negligent medical treatment of an injury is not normally a novus actus unless it is so unreasonable as to eclipse the original wrong (compare Knightley v Johns). So Ali/Speedy and Dr Dee are likely to be concurrently liable for the limp. Ben can recover the whole from either, and they can seek contribution from each other under the Civil Liability (Contribution) Act 1978, with shares based on responsibility (s 2(1)).

Cara. She was not in physical danger, so she is a secondary victim and must satisfy Alcock. As Ben's mother, a close tie of love and affection is presumed. She saw Ben at the hospital an hour after the accident, still untreated and in great pain; in McLoughlin v O'Brian a mother arriving at hospital about two hours later was within the immediate aftermath. She perceived it with her own senses, and she has a recognised psychiatric illness; such injury to a parent of reasonable fortitude seeing this is foreseeable. Paul v Royal Wolverhampton [2024] UKSC 1 requires an 'accident', an external event causing injury. The road collision is such an accident, so her claim against Ali and Speedy is likely to succeed. Paul would prevent her claiming as a secondary victim against Dr Dee for any distress caused by the medical delay itself.

questions.q: 'The modern law of vicarious liability has expanded too far and become unpredictable.' Discuss with reference to the decisions of the Supreme Court since 2012.
markScheme: Explains the two-stage test and the rationale of vicarious liability (enterprise risk, loss-spreading, deterrence)
Stage 1 expansion: CCWS (2012), Cox (2016), Armes (2017); policy factors
Stage 1 limits: Barclays (2020) independent contractor; BXB (2023) restates
Stage 2 development: Lister close connection; Dubai Aluminium; Mohamud (2016) 'field of activities' and 'unbroken sequence'
Stage 2 retrenchment: Morrison (2020) personal vendetta; BXB (2023) no close connection
Evaluates predictability: evaluative tests, policy factors, abuse cases; insurance implications
Considers alternatives (non-delegable duties, Woodland) and whether expansion is justified for abuse victims
Reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Vicarious liability imposes strict liability on one person for another's tort. Its standard justifications are enterprise risk, loss-spreading through insurance, and deterrence. The test now has two stages: a relationship of employment or one akin to it, and a close connection between that relationship and the tort (BXB [2023] UKSC 15).

Expansion was real. In Various Claimants v Catholic Child Welfare Society [2012] UKSC 56 the Supreme Court held a religious institute liable for abuse by brothers who were not its employees, setting out policy features (ability to pay, activity on the defendant's behalf and integral to its business, creation of risk, control). Cox v Ministry of Justice [2016] applied this to a prisoner working in a prison kitchen, and Armes v Nottinghamshire CC [2017] to foster parents. At stage 2, Lister v Hesley Hall [2001] had replaced the Salmond formula with a close connection test, and Mohamud v WM Morrison [2016] appeared to loosen it further, asking about the employee's 'field of activities' and an 'unbroken sequence of events' and referring to social justice. Critics argued that these policy-laden, evaluative formulations made outcomes hard to predict and pushed liability onto bodies whose link to the wrongdoing was tenuous.

The Supreme Court has since reined this in. Barclays Bank v Various Claimants [2020] UKSC 13 reaffirmed that there is no liability for a true independent contractor carrying on its own business, and treated the Christian Brothers factors as aids to deciding whether a relationship is akin to employment, not free-standing policy tests. WM Morrison v Various Claimants [2020] UKSC 12 held that Mohamud had not changed the law: the question is still whether the wrongful conduct was so closely connected with authorised acts that it may fairly and properly be regarded as done in the ordinary course of employment (Dubai Aluminium), and an employee pursuing a personal vendetta against his employer was outside it. BXB [2023] then restated both stages, cautioned against jumping to policy, and denied liability because the elder's rape was connected to a family friendship rather than to his role.

Predictability is therefore better than the proposition suggests, but not perfect. Both stages remain evaluative, especially in abuse cases where Lister and Armes favour liability and BXB does not. Whether a relationship is 'akin to employment' in new forms of work, such as gig platforms, remains open. Some of the expansion is defensible: abuse victims often have no solvent defendant other than the institution that gave the abuser access and authority.

In conclusion, the law did expand significantly between 2012 and 2017, and the language of Mohamud invited unpredictability. The 2020 and 2023 decisions have restored structure by anchoring stage 1 in the employment analogy and stage 2 in the Dubai Aluminium formula. The better view is that the law has expanded in a principled direction, driven by enterprise risk and the abuse cases, but remains fact-sensitive by nature.
